'''Noah Scott Herron''' (born April 3, 1982) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] in the seventh round of the [[2005 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Northwestern Wildcats football|Northwestern Wildcats]].

Herron was also a member of the [[Green Bay Packers]], [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], [[New York Jets]], [[Cleveland Browns]], [[New York Sentinels]], and [[Hartford Colonials]].

'''Norris Lee Weese''' (August 12, 1951 – January 20, 1995) was a professional [[American football]] [[quarterback]]. He was a star quarterback for [[Chalmette High School]] and the [[University of Mississippi]]. He had the unenviable task of succeeding Mississippi QB legend [[Archie Manning]], but performed well in the key position.

Recalling the November 4, 1972 game in [[Baton Rouge, Louisiana|Baton Rouge]] in which Ole Miss lost to [[Louisiana State University]], 17–16, because of a unique touchdown catch from quarterback [[Bert Jones]] to LSU running back Brad Davis, Weese said [[Tiger Stadium (LSU)|Tiger Stadium]] "just exploded with thousands of fans jumping high in the night air." Until that point the Rebels had outplayed LSU all night long.<ref>Chet Hilburn, ''The Mystique of Tiger Stadium: 25 Greatest Games: The Ascension of LSU Football'' ([[Bloomington, Indiana]]: WestBow Press, 2012), pp. 37-38</ref>

Weese played the 1974 season for [[The Hawaiians (WFL)|The Hawaiians]] in the [[World Football League]] before joining the [[NFL]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mmbolding.com/BSR/pqWFL74Weese.htm |title=WFL Starting Quarterbacks |publisher=mmbolding.com |access-date=October 2, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110105152017/http://www.mmbolding.com/BSR/pqWFL74Weese.htm |archive-date=January 5, 2011 }}</ref> He spent four seasons in the NFL playing for the [[Denver Broncos]] (1976–1979), mostly as a backup quarterback.

In [[Super Bowl XII]] against the [[Dallas Cowboys]], where his famed high school head coach Bobby Nuss held the chains, Weese replaced starter [[Craig Morton]] in the third quarter after Morton nearly threw his 5th interception.<ref name="washingtonpost">{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/sports/nfl/longterm/superbowl/stories/sb12.htm |title=Super Bowl XII Cowboys Rip Erring Broncos |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=January 15, 1978 |access-date=October 2, 2010}}</ref> Weese led the Broncos to a touchdown on the drive to cut his team's deficit to 20–10, but he lost a fumble in the fourth quarter, setting up a Dallas touchdown that put the game away.<ref name="washingtonpost"/> He was known for being a mobile QB.

Weese was named [[Starting lineup|starting]] quarterback for the Broncos in 1979, but a knee injury that year ended his NFL career. He finished his career with 1887 passing yards, seven touchdowns and fourteen interceptions.

Weese went on to become a [[certified public accountant]] in [[Denver, Colorado]].

Norris Weese died on January 20, 1995, of [[bone cancer]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=990CE6DE153EF937A15752C0A963958260 |title=Norris Weese; Broncos Quarterback, 43 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=January 24, 1995 |access-date=October 2, 2010}}</ref>

To this day, Weese holds the record for most single game rushing yards as a quarterback in Broncos history, rushing for 120 yards on 12 carries against the [[Chicago Bears]] on December 12, 1976.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197612120chi.htm|title = Denver Broncos at Chicago Bears - December 12th, 1976| website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/play-index/pgl_finder.cgi?request=1&match=game&year_min=1950&year_max=2016&season_start=1&season_end=-1&age_min=0&age_max=0&pos=0&game_type=R&team_id=den&career_game_num_min=0&career_game_num_max=499&game_num_min=0&game_num_max=99&week_num_min=0&week_num_max=99&c1stat=pass_att&c1comp=gt&c1val=10&c2stat=rush_yds&c2comp=gt&c2val=60&c3stat=choose&c3comp=gt&c4stat=choose&c4comp=gt&c5comp=choose&c5gtlt=lt&c6mult=1.0&c6comp=choose&order_by=rush_yds|title=Player Game Finder Query Results|website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref>

'''Nnamdi Asomugha''' ({{Audio|LL-Q33578_(ibo)-Goodymeraj-Nnamdi_Asomugha.wav|Listen|help=no}}; born July 6, 1981) is a Nigerian-American actor, director, producer, and former professional [[American football|football]] [[cornerback]] who played 11 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) with the [[Oakland Raiders]], [[Philadelphia Eagles]], and [[San Francisco 49ers]].
